findings.what: The screen never says the lesson's main point: the pull's angle is a direction, but the phasor's angle is a moment in the cycle. That point appears only in step 2's hidden Why and the finish line, so the screen should lead with it, for example 'The pull's angle is a direction. The turning arrow's angle is a time: frozen at 45°, it is 2.5 ms into the cycle.'

'They turn together, so the sum's height is always their two heights added' gives the wrong cause, because heights add nose to tail for any two arrows. Turning together is what keeps the sum the same length and turning with them, so write 'At every instant the sum's height is their two heights added. They turn together, so the sum turns with them.'

The screen says the gap 'is the neutral current' without the reason: whatever the three lines carry out must come back on the neutral, so the neutral carries their nose-to-tail sum. That is the one step that makes the picture mean something electrically, and it is skipped.

'Three equal 10 A currents ... so the neutral carries 0 A' reads as an absolute. On a real board, harmonics from electronic loads add up in the neutral even when the board is balanced, and 150 Hz is the very arrow from step 5. Add a short qualifier such as 'With pure 50 Hz sine waves'; the explain and ignores fields already carry the caveat.

findings.where: Step 11 (All three differ), hint for '4 A'
findings.what: The hint names 'the difference rule', but no screen ever states it. Step 10's Why works only by parts, so either state the rule there ('When two lines match, the neutral carries the difference: 10 − 4 = 6 A.') or reword the hint.

The brief promised the lesson would say once, as contested, that phasors here are drawn at rms while the turning arrow's length is the peak, but no screen says it ('contested' is null). Step 3's 'heights now … A' treats 3 A as a peak, step 12's 230 V is an rms value, and nothing tells him the arrow's length changed meaning.

The balanced closed triangle and its 0 A readout show for only about 0.3 s: the readout arrives at 2.7 s and L2 starts shrinking at 3.0 s. Holding the balanced state for about a second before the shrink would let the first half of the idea register.

findings.where: Steps 1, 3 and 5, act line and Turn/Freeze button
findings.what: While the opening demonstration plays (about 5 s), the button reads 'Freeze' but the line under the picture says 'Press Turn it to set the arrow going', so the instruction names a button that is not on screen yet.
The screen says a phasor can be divided but leaves out the contrast that makes this a difference: a force arrow cannot be divided like this. One short sentence would say it.
398 V is √3 × 230, the line voltage he knows as 400 V from AC circuits, and one closing sentence saying so would tie the puzzle to his trade.

The brief's power point never reaches a screen, only the practice list. VI cos φ has the dot product's shape, but multiplying phasors as numbers adds their angles, and lesson 5 already set this up with a voltage and a current.
'Freeze it and you have the phasor' reads as an instruction in the read-through. 'Frozen at one instant, it is the phasor, the fixed arrow r∠θ' reads the same with or without the button.
The ray from the arrow's tip to the wave is amber, a colour kept for what is due and for key terms. Ink, dashed, as the brief asks for shadows, would keep to the colour rule.

The bold summary line carries [^1], which is not a figure he would look up. 'Ordinary vector rules give no way to divide one vector by another' rests on a forum answer [^3]. Drop the footnote on the summary line, and cite a textbook for the division point or leave it unfootnoted.
